teaser: Quiet water on a leaf. Follow the night’s hidden steps.
title: The drops that did not fall.
question: No rain fell. Why is this leaf wet?
idea: Water vapor in the air can condense into dew on a cool leaf. Sunrise warms the leaf, and the drops evaporate.

curiosity.intro: Follow one small clue. Make a guess, then look again.
curiosity.carryForward: Read the leaf’s story, follow a counting command, and try a night in the dew diorama.

questions.question: Can a leaf get wet without rain?
questions.notice: Look at the drops on the leaf and the nearby spider web.
questions.say: Yes. Air holds invisible water vapor. Dew forms right on a cool surface when that vapor condenses into liquid drops. It does not fall from the sky like rain.
questions.try: Point to where the drops sit. Imagine a drop growing there, instead of falling down.

questions.question: How does a leaf cool during the night?
questions.notice: The leaf faces a wide, clear sky. The grass is still.
questions.say: Surfaces give off heat to the sky. On a clear, calm night, a leaf can lose heat and get colder than the air around it. Clouds and wind can slow that cooling.
questions.try: Trace the leaf’s edge. Say the first command: “Cool the leaf.”

questions.question: Where was the water before we saw drops?
questions.notice: The air above the leaf looks clear. New beads cling to the leaf.
questions.say: The water was invisible vapor in the air. Air touching the cool leaf cools too. At its dew point, it is cool enough that it cannot keep all its water invisible. Some vapor condenses into liquid dew.
questions.try: Imagine clear air touching this leaf. Use “condense” to tell what changed.

questions.question: Where do the drops go after sunrise?
questions.notice: Sunlight reaches the leaf. Fewer drops remain.
questions.say: As the sun warms the leaf, liquid water evaporates back into invisible vapor. The water changes form; it does not vanish forever. A cold glass can collect drops on its outside for the same condensation reason: that water comes from the surrounding air.
questions.try: Say two commands in order: “Warm the leaf. Watch the drops shrink.”

reading.title: Little’s instructions for dew
reading.coverText: A wet leaf. A dry path. Little Wonderer follows the night’s hidden instructions to solve a morning mystery.
reading.foldableTitle: A little book of morning dew.
reading.parentNote: Age 7 / Grade 2. Read six short scenes at Leo’s pace. Pause for a guess, then connect each new word to the leaf. Welcome shared reading and spoken answers.

outline.arc: Little Wonderer investigates a leaf wet without rain, traces night cooling and condensation, records the steps like a program, then sees sunrise reverse the change through evaporation.

beatIntents.intent: Discover wet leaf and web before sunrise despite no rain; establish the mystery.
Reconstruct clear calm night and leaf cooling to open sky; instruction 1.
Close view shows onset of dew, with invisible vapor explained in prose; instruction 2.
Inspect drops formed on leaf and nearby web; condensation and instruction 3.
Little records ordered commands in a notebook; connect instructions with a program.
Sunrise warms the same leaf; remaining beads shrink by evaporation; instruction 4.

beats.title: A quiet puzzle
beats.passage: Before sunrise, Little Wonderer found tiny drops on a leaf. A spider web beside it wore shining beads. “Did I miss the rain?” Little asked. The path was dry. Big Wonderer knelt beside the leaf. “Let’s follow the clues back through the night.”
beats.prompt: Which clue makes the drops a mystery?

beats.title: The open night
beats.passage: The night had been clear and calm. The leaf gave off heat to the open sky. It cooled and could get colder than the air around it. Little began a list of nature’s instructions: “1. Cool the leaf.” Nothing had fallen from the sky.
beats.prompt: Where did the leaf give off heat?

beats.title: Water we cannot see
beats.passage: Air holds water vapor, water in a gas form we cannot see. Air touching the cool leaf cooled too. At the dew point, it was cool enough that it could not keep all its water invisible. Little added: “2. Wait for the air to touch it.”
beats.prompt: What water was already in the air?

beats.title: Beads on a thread
beats.passage: Tiny drops formed right on the leaf. Water vapor had begun to condense: it changed from a gas into liquid water. That water was dew. The cool spider web held beads too. “3. Look for tiny drops,” Little wrote. “They formed here. They did not fall like rain!”

beats.title: Little’s instructions
beats.passage: Little checked the order: cool the leaf, let air touch it, then notice dew. “My commands are like a little program,” Little said. “But nature does not read my notebook!” Big smiled. The instructions helped Little explain the changes, one step at a time.
beats.prompt: Why does the order of the commands matter?

beats.title: Back into the air
beats.passage: Sunrise warmed the leaf. The beads grew smaller as water began to evaporate: it changed from liquid back into invisible vapor. Little added one last command: “4. Warm the leaf.” The water was not gone forever. It had returned to the air. What would the next night bring?
beats.prompt: Where can the water go after sunrise?

math.title: Six clues to count
math.intro: These are pretend counts from Little’s notebook. Solve one question at a time. Real drops do not form in neat rows or grow by a fixed counting rule.

tasks.prompt: Little counts 38 dew drops on one leaf and 47 on another. How many drops are there altogether?
tasks.hint: Add 8 and 7 ones. Trade 10 ones for 1 ten.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: A spider web has 72 dew beads. After sunrise, 38 evaporate. How many beads remain?
tasks.hint: Trade 1 ten for 10 ones. Subtract 8 from 12, then subtract the tens.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: A leaf has 28 drops. Then 17 more form, and later 19 evaporate. How many drops remain?
tasks.hint: First find how many drops there are after 17 form. Then subtract 19.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Little draws 4 rows of dew beads with 6 beads in each row. How many beads does Little draw?
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Little has drawn 27 drops and wants 60 in the notebook. How many more drops must Little draw?
tasks.hint: Count up from 27 to 30. Then count from 30 to 60.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: Follow Little’s drawing command: add 5 drops each time. The counts are 12, 17, 22. What count comes next?
tasks.hint: Repeat the same instruction: add 5 to the last count.
tasks.worked: 22 + 5 = 27. The instruction adds 5 at each step.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: The command “add 5 drops” makes a drawing pattern. Nature does not follow these pretend numbers.
math.parentNote: Age 7 / Grade 2 stretch. Six tasks cover the learning contract. Offer counters, tens-and-ones sketches, or oral reasoning. Pause between pages; completing all six at once is optional.
math.printNote: All numbers are pretend. Draw, use tens and ones, or show your steps.

writing.title: Give the leaf an instruction.
writing.intro: Choose one scene below. Write one command sentence for the leaf’s story. You may add a second step.
writing.draw: Draw the leaf before or after your command. Add one label.

frames.hint: tell the leaf what to do before dew forms
tell what to notice on the cool leaf
tell what to watch as the leaf warms

writing.check: Read your sentence. Does it tell what to do, using a command such as Cool, Wait, Look, or Watch?
writing.parentNote: Accept Leo’s spoken command, dictation, invented spelling, or writing. One clear sentence is enough. Example: “First cool the leaf, then wait for tiny drops.”

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: The leaf and spider web were wet, but the path was dry and no rain had fallen. These clues made Little investigate another source of water.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: The leaf must become cool enough first. Air touching it cools; water vapor can then condense into drops. Cooling comes before noticing dew.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: The drops evaporated: liquid water changed back into invisible water vapor in the air.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept one sensible command sentence, spoken, dictated, or written. Example: “First cool the leaf, then wait for tiny drops.” The notebook describes nature; it does not control the weather.

parentGuidance: Leo is 7, in Grade 2. Follow his questions and welcome dictation. Dew forms on cool surfaces; it does not fall like rain. “Air holds vapor” is kid-sized language: the air is not a sponge. Cooling to the dew point allows vapor to condense. Clear skies favor radiative cooling; clouds and wind can reduce it, but do not guarantee a dry leaf. All math counts and diorama temperatures are pretend. No experiment is required. A cold glass is an analogy, not a required activity.

sources.label: NOAA / National Weather Service · dew and frost development

authoring.learningRule: Leo is age 7, Grade 2. New Curiosity packs require exactly six math tasks, one per skill: addition-regrouping, subtraction-regrouping, two-step, equal-groups, missing-addend, pattern-sequencing. Numbers and results stay within 100. Each task asks one clear question and includes a hint, numeric answer, and short worked step. Equal groups needs repeated-addition support. Tie the pattern or sequence to the day's theme. Explain precise vocabulary in context; welcome speech and dictation.

titleCard.subtitle: A leaf, a quiet night, and water we could not see.

visualNotes.intent: Six imagined garden scenes follow one broad leaf, a nearby spider web, and Big and Little Wonderer from a puzzling wet morning through the night’s hidden steps to sunrise.
visualNotes.grownUpNote: Water vapor is invisible. Enlarged drops are an illustration aid; the math counts are invented. The diorama’s temperatures and timing are a simplified model, not a weather forecast.

quiz.title: Four clues to keep
quiz.intro: Think about the same leaf. Choose one answer for each clue.

choices: Water in a gas form we cannot see
questions.answer: Water vapor is invisible water in a gas form.

questions.prompt: What helps the leaf cool on a clear, calm night?
choices: Heat leaving the leaf for the open sky
The leaf making its own ice
questions.answer: The leaf gives off heat to the open sky and can become colder than the surrounding air.

questions.prompt: What happens when air touching the leaf cools to its dew point?
choices: Some water vapor condenses into liquid drops on the leaf
Rain must fall from the sky
questions.answer: Some vapor condenses into liquid dew right on the leaf. At the dew point, the air is cool enough for condensation.

questions.prompt: What happens as sunrise warms the dew?
choices: The drops turn into invisible water vapor
The drops turn into pieces of leaf
The drops must rise as tiny liquid balls
questions.answer: Liquid dew evaporates into invisible water vapor. The water changes form; it is not gone forever.
